item.title: The Legend of Sargon of Akkad: Inspiration for the Story of Moses
item.description: The Legend of Sargon of Akkad describes the king's humble origins and rise to power with the help of the goddess Ishtar and concludes with a challenge to future kings to go where he has gone and do as he has done. Sargon was the founder of the first multinational empire in the world, whose reign became legendary, inspiring many tales about him. item.title: Secession of the Plebs: One of History's First Class Conflicts
item.description: In 494 BCE, the plebeians (commoners) protested their mistreatment by the ruling patrician class with a mass exodus from Rome. Leaving the patricians to fend for themselves, they set up camp on the Sacred Mountain three miles (5 km) away and forced the Senate to negotiate. Discover how Rome's plebeians won their rights through some of the first mass general strikes in Western history.

item.title: Cuneiform: The Writing System That Made History
item.description: Cuneiform is a system of writing first developed by the ancient Sumerians of Mesopotamia circa 3600/3500 BCE. It is considered the most significant among the many cultural contributions of the Sumerians and the greatest among those of the Sumerian city of Uruk, which further developed and advanced cuneiform circa 3200 BCE and allowed for the creation of literature.

item.title: Script: The Written Record of Humanity
item.description: A writing system is listed as one of the five factors necessary for the development of civilization. Although frequently taken for granted in the present day, script has been vital to the progress of humanity. Script has served to communicate the most profound, as well as the most practical, aspects of the human condition. item.title: Liberty's Grid: A Founding Father, a Mathematical Dreamland, and the Shaping of America
item.description: A bird’s eye view of the U.S. reveals perpendicular streets, rectangular fields, and uniformity in both urban and rural landscapes. "Liberty’s Grid" examines how this gridded landscape came to exist. It explores how the work of Isaac Newton and René Descartes shaped Thomas Jefferson’s ideas. It also shows how grids produced a backlash in favor of non-gridded landscapes. This book is well suited for both scholars and students and is highly recommended.

item.title: Battle of Rorke's Drift: Heroic Stand of the Anglo-Zulu War
item.description: Immediately after their famous victory over the British at the Battle of Isandlwana on 22 January 1879, as many as 4,000 Zulu warriors pushed on across the Zulu-Natal border. This Zulu army headed for Rorke's Drift, some 12 miles (19 km) away. Here was a mission station and 140 soldiers of the 24th Warwickshire Regiment and allied troops. item.title: Civilization: From Nomadic Life to the Farm and City
item.description: Civilization (from the Latin civis=citizen and civitas=city) is a term applied to any society which has developed a writing system, government, production of surplus food, division of labor, and urbanization. The term is difficult to define because not all "civilizations" include every one of the above facets. The term is often used, therefore, to suggest a highly developed culture.

item.title: Sargon and Ur-Zababa: Two Dream Visions and a River of Blood
item.description: The poem Sargon and Ur-Zababa relates how Sargon was chosen by the gods to fulfill his destiny by overthrowing Ur-Zababa, even though, as the work begins, Sargon himself seems content as Ur-Zababa's servant, oblivious to the gods' plans. item.title: Enheduanna: The World's First Author Known by Name
item.description: Poetess Enheduanna (c. 2300 BCE) is credited with creating the paradigms of poetry, psalms, and prayers used throughout the ancient world which led to the development of the genres recognized in the present day. item.title: American Crusade: Christianity, Warfare, and National Identity, 1860–1920
item.description: Wetzel’s "American Crusade: Christianity, Warfare, and National Identity, 1860–1920" is aimed at the scholarly reader and examines how religious ideology and social location shaped how American Christians viewed war in relation to their national identity. The book does an excellent job outlining Congregationalist views and the preaching of Lyman Abbott. It is a worthwhile source for those looking for a deeper understanding of the link between Christian Nationalism and American identity.
